eras.title: Mesoamerica's first civilisation
eras.text: In the swampy lowlands of Mexico's Gulf Coast, the Olmec build San Lorenzo and La Venta and carve colossal basalt heads. Their gods, ball game and calendar influence every later Mesoamerican culture.

eras.title: Preclassic Maya
eras.text: Maya villages grow into cities such as El Mirador with huge pyramids; writing and the Long Count calendar appear.

eras.title: Classic Maya
eras.text: Dozens of rival city-states — Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán — ruled by divine kings fill the lowlands of Guatemala, Mexico and Belize. The Maya develop the Americas' only full writing system, advanced astronomy and the concept of zero.

eras.title: Postclassic Maya
eras.text: After the southern cities collapse, Chichén Itzá and then Mayapán dominate the Yucatán, which fragments into small states before the Spanish conquest.

eras.title: Resistance under Spanish rule
eras.text: The Spanish conquest of the Maya is slow and hard-fought; the last independent Maya city, Nojpetén, falls only in 1697.

eras.title: City of the Gods
eras.text: One of the largest cities in the ancient world (up to 100,000 people), with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. Its influence reaches the Maya cities; it is burned and abandoned around 550.

eras.title: Monte Albán
eras.text: The Zapotecs build their hilltop capital in the Oaxaca valley, one of Mesoamerica's first cities, with early writing.

eras.title: Zapotecs and Mixtecs
eras.text: After the decline of Monte Albán, Zapotec communities continue to flourish in the Valley of Oaxaca until the Spanish conquest of 1521.

eras.title: The Toltecs
eras.text: From their capital Tula, the Toltecs dominate central Mexico; the Aztecs later revere them as the originators of civilisation.

eras.title: The rise of the Mexica
eras.text: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco and serve as mercenaries for more powerful neighbours.

eras.title: The Triple Alliance
eras.text: Three Nahua city-states — Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan — form the Triple Alliance after a civil war. Tenochtitlan becomes dominant, and the alliance conquers most of central Mexico, collecting tribute through its own officials, until the Spanish and their native allies defeat it in 1521.

eras.title: Tawantinsuyu
eras.text: From Cusco, Pachacuti and his successors conquer the Andes from Ecuador to Chile — the largest empire in the Americas — linked by 40,000 km of roads, administered with knotted-string khipus and without money or markets.

eras.title: Civil war and conquest
eras.text: A smallpox epidemic and a civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar leave the empire vulnerable to Pizarro (1532). A rump Inca state survives at Vilcabamba until 1572.

eras.title: The Chimú
eras.text: A coastal Peruvian kingdom whose adobe capital Chan Chan is the largest city of the pre-Columbian Americas; the Inca conquer it around 1470.

eras.title: The Moche
eras.text: A civilisation of Peru's north coast, famous for irrigation, huge adobe pyramids and lifelike portrait pottery.

eras.title: The Nazca
eras.text: A culture of the river valleys of Peru's arid southern coast, known for its ceramics and textiles, the Nazca Lines (immense designs in the desert whose purpose is unknown) and underground aqueducts, some still working today.

eras.title: The Wari
eras.text: A Middle Horizon civilization that flourishes in the highlands and coast of modern Peru from about 500 to 1000 AD, ruled from its capital Wari, near modern Ayacucho.

eras.title: Chavín
eras.text: A religious culture centred on the temple at Chavín de Huántar in the Peruvian Andes, whose art spreads widely.

eras.title: Hopewell
eras.text: Peoples of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys build great geometric earthworks and trade obsidian, copper and shells across North America.

eras.title: New Spain
eras.text: Spain's viceroyalty rules Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and (via Manila) the Philippines. Silver from Zacatecas and Potosí fuels world trade while Indigenous populations collapse from epidemics.

eras.title: Thirteen colonies
eras.text: English colonies stretch along the Atlantic coast, growing tobacco and rice with enslaved African labour in the South and trading and farming in the North.

eras.title: Independence and expansion
eras.text: The Thirteen Colonies rebel against British taxes and the Intolerable Acts, declare independence in 1776 and win it in the Revolutionary War. The new country expands west, displacing Native nations, and the Civil War ends slavery.

eras.title: Industrial giant
eras.text: Railways, immigration and industry make the US the world's largest economy by 1900. It decides both world wars.

eras.title: Superpower
eras.text: The US leads the West in the Cold War, lands on the Moon (1969) and after 1991 is the sole superpower.

eras.title: New France
eras.text: French fur traders and missionaries settle along the St Lawrence; Britain conquers New France in the Seven Years' War.

eras.title: Dominion of Canada
eras.text: Canada becomes a self-governing confederation in 1867 and gradually gains full independence.

eras.title: Independent Mexico
eras.text: After independence from Spain in 1821, Mexico faces conflicts between caudillos (strongmen), the Mexican–American War and a French invasion, before the long rule of Porfirio Díaz.

eras.title: Revolution and modern Mexico
eras.text: The Mexican Revolution is followed by 70 years of one-party rule and then multiparty democracy.

eras.title: Colonial Brazil
eras.text: Portugal builds a sugar colony worked by millions of enslaved Africans; gold rushes in Minas Gerais follow. The Portuguese court moves to Rio in 1808.

eras.title: Empire and republic
eras.text: Brazil becomes an independent empire (1822), abolishes slavery last in the Americas (1888) and becomes a republic (1889).

eras.title: Argentina
eras.text: Argentina declares independence on 9 July 1816; after the defeat of the Spanish in 1824, a federal state, today's Argentine Republic, is formed in 1853–1861.

eras.title: Paleo-Inuit (Dorset)
eras.text: The Dorset people live across the Canadian Arctic and Greenland, hunting seals and walrus.

eras.title: Thule — ancestors of the Inuit
eras.text: The Thule people, precursors of all modern Inuit, develop in coastal Alaska by 1000 AD and spread east across northern Canada, reaching Greenland by the 13th century and replacing the Dorset. They were in contact with the Norse.

eras.title: Voyagers of the Pacific
eras.text: Austronesian navigators in double-hulled canoes settle Tonga and Samoa, then the far islands of Polynesia — the greatest feat of ocean exploration before modern times.

eras.title: Polynesian societies
eras.text: Polynesians settle the far corners of the Polynesian Triangle, including Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and New Zealand, where Māori ancestors arrive between about 1320 and 1350.

eras.title: The oldest living cultures
eras.text: Aboriginal Australians and Torres Strait Islanders have lived on the continent for at least 50,000 years, with hundreds of languages, complex kinship systems, land management by fire and Dreaming traditions.

eras.title: Colonisation and the modern nation
eras.text: British colonisation begins in 1788. Over the following century and a half the Aboriginal population falls sharply, while the British colonies unite as the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901.
